The derivation begins with the vague form of spatiality as a foundational sensory datum, which is inherently unordered. This is modeled as a manifold S(Q) where Q denotes qualitative sensations. The unordered nature implies that no internal ordering mechanism exists within the raw sensory input. The second primitive, unordered spatial perception U, captures this lack of structure. It is a function of sensory input alone, independent of cognitive interpretation. The third primitive, intellectual space synthesis I(O), introduces the cognitive act required to transform U into an ordered space O. This process is non-trivial and involves complex neural computations. The synthesis is a mapping from the unordered domain to the ordered domain, represented as I: U → O. The failure mode occurs when I cannot adequately process U, leading to perceptual disarray or misalignment between sensory input and cognitive model. The duality arises between the sensory and cognitive layers—where sensory input is the base and cognitive synthesis provides structure. The epistemological gap lies in the transition from raw sensation to structured cognition, which requires recursive mental operations.
